blocks.text: Where the sacer ales [sacred bird] is ἱέραξ [hierax]; as in Demetrius, in the Preface to the Hieracosophium: Τῷ τῶν ἱερῶν ὀρνίθων γένει πρὸς σωτηρίαν τινὰ πορίσασθαι μηχανὴν [Tō tōn hierōn ornithōn genei pros sōtērian tina porisasthai mēchanēn], "to find some art for the preservation of the race of sacred birds." And again: Ἐσπούδασά τινα χρήσιμον θεραπείαν πρὸς σωτηρίαν τῷ ἱερῷ τῶν ὀρνίθων γένει καταλιπεῖν [Espoudasa tina chrēsimon therapeian pros sōtērian tō hierō tōn ornithōn genei katalipein], "I have endeavoured to leave to the sacred race of birds some useful treatment for its preservation." In these words it is plain that by sacred birds and the race of sacred birds τοὺς ἱέρακας [tous hierakas], that is, hawks, are meant. "And why the hawk is so called in Greek," says Servius, "is not without a reason, which is known to those versed in sacred rites." I would think this arose from the superstition of the Egyptians, for whom among the sacred animals none was so sacred as the ibis and the hawk. Thus, if anyone had killed some other animal unwillingly, he was fined at the discretion of the priests. Ὃς δ' ἂν ἶβιν, ἢ ἴρηκα ἀποκτένῃ, ἤν τε ἑκὼν, ἤν τε ἀέκων, τεθνάναι ἀνάγκη [Hos d' an ibin, ē irēka apoktenē, ēn te hekōn, ēn te aekōn, tethnanai anankē]; "But whoever had killed an ibis or a hawk, whether willingly or unwillingly, had to die." So it stands in the Euterpe of Herodotus [ch. 65].

Indeed, even today they count the sacer among the species of hawks or falcons. But, to say what the matter really is, the word is not Latin but Arabic: صقر [ṣaqr] or سقر [saqr] or زقر [zaqr], as some write it with Sin and with Ze, although it is more often written with Sad, from the verb صقر [ṣaqara] sakara, which means to see sharply, just like the Chaldee סכר sekar. The Kamus: الصاقر حديد البصر [al-ṣāqir ḥadīd al-baṣar] Sakir, "one who is sharp-sighted." Thus الصقر [al-ṣaqr], the noun derived from it (French sacre), first signifies كل طاير يصيد [kull ṭāyir yaṣīd], every bird used in fowling. Secondly, one of the four species of birds of prey. These are namely صقر [ṣaqr] sacer, شاهين [shāhīn] sahin, عقاب [ʿuqāb] okab, and بازي [bāzī] bazi. And the صقر [ṣaqr] sacer is subdivided into three further species: namely the صقر [ṣaqr] sacer properly so called, the كونج [kawnaj] chauneg, and the يويو [yūyū] [col. 268] juju. To describe each of these here would be long and tedious. Therefore we shall treat only of the sacer properly so called. It is otherwise called اجدل [ajdal] agdal, robust; اكدر [akdar] achdar, dusky; and قماطي [qumāṭī] kumati, greedy for flesh; and it is described by Damir and others thus: هو من الجوارح بمنزلة البغال من الدواب لانه اصبر علي الشدة واحمل الغليظ الاذي واحسن القاء واشد اقدام علي جملة من الكركي وغيره ومزاجه ابرد من ساير ما تقدم ذكره من الحوارح وارطب وبهذا السبب يضرا علي الغزال والارنب وهو اهدي من البازي نفسا واسرع بالناس انسا واكثر منة [III, 8] منه قنعا ولبرد مزاجه لا يشرب ماء ولو اقام دهرا وكذلك يوصف بالبخر ونتي الفم وله كفان في يده كالسبع لانه يكف بهما علي ما اخذ اي يجمع [huwa min al-jawāriḥ bi-manzilat al-bighāl min al-dawābb li-annahu aṣbar ʿalā al-shidda wa-aḥmal al-ghalīẓ al-adhā wa-aḥsan ilqāʾ wa-ashadd iqdām ʿalā jumla min al-kurkī wa-ghayrihi wa-mizājuhu abrad min sāyir mā taqaddama dhikruhu min al-ḥawāriḥ wa-arṭab wa-bi-hādhā al-sabab yuḍrā ʿalā al-ghazāl wa-al-arnab wa-huwa ahdā min al-bāzī nafsan wa-asraʿ bi-al-nās unsan wa-akthar mna minhu qanaʿan wa-li-bard mizājihi lā yashrab māʾ wa-law aqāma dahran wa-kadhālika yūṣaf bi-al-bakhar wa-ntī al-fam wa-lahu kaffān fī yadihi ka-al-sabuʿ li-annahu yakuff bihimā ʿalā mā akhadha ay yajmaʿ], "It stands to the other birds of prey as the mule to the other beasts of burden. For it is stronger, more able to bear heavier injuries, better in attack, and firmer of foot against every kind of crane and birds of that sort. And it is of a colder and also moister temperament than the other birds of prey treated above. Therefore it is trained for hunting gazelles and hares." And than the bazi, or hawk, it is more docile, is tamed by men more quickly, and is more easily satisfied. Because of the coldness of its temperament it never drinks water, however long it remains (without drink). Hence it is described as having a fetid and foul-smelling mouth. In its foot it has palms like wild beasts, with which it pounces on what it catches and holds it." Alkazuinius writes that no hunting by birds of prey is so marvellous as when two sacres, flying at a gazelle's eyes or beating it with their wings, detain it until it falls into the hunters' hands. He also marvels that so small a bird لشجاعة خلقها الله تعالي فيه [li-shajāʿa khalaqahā Allāh taʿālā fīhi], "because of the boldness which God Most High has put in it," dares to leap upon a crane, which is of so much greater bulk. The first originator of this kind of fowling among the Arabs was Alharits, son of Muawiya. So much in passing about the sacer ^{(1)}.

Callimachus reckons six kinds of hawks, Aristotle ten, Pliny sixteen. But by size they are reduced to two, of which the Philosopher speaks in book 8, chapter 3 of the History: Ἱέρακες ἄμφω, ὅτε φαβοτύπος, καὶ ὁ σπιζίας, διαφέρουσι τὸ μέγεθος πολὺ ἀλλήλων [Hierakes amphō, hote phabotypos, kai ho spizias, diapherousi to megethos poly allēlōn]; "Both hawks, namely the dove-hawk and the finch-hawk, differ much from each other in size." The former more recent writers call astur (French autour); the latter nisus and sparverius. Iulius Firmicus indeed mentions asturs [col. 269] in book 5, chapter 7. But the name nisus seems taken from the Hebrew נץ nets, or from the Chaldee נצה netsa. To the same is referred the metamorphosis of Nisus, king of the Megarians, although the poets feign that he was changed not into a hawk but into a sea eagle. Ovid, in book 8 of the Metamorphoses:
